blocks.text: Palm wine turns sour after a day, lime juice stings a cut, and wood ash rubbed on the skin feels slippery. Long before anyone wrote a chemical equation, people were sorting substances into acids and bases by taste and touch. Chemistry gives the same distinction a precise, testable definition.

blocks.title: Two definitions you must know
blocks.text: Arrhenius: an acid produces hydrogen ions, H+, as the only positive ions in aqueous solution, and a base produces hydroxide ions, OH-, as the only negative ions. Bronsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. The Bronsted-Lowry model is wider because it does not require water.

blocks.markdown:
## Acids

In water an acid ionises to release hydrogen ions, which immediately attach to water molecules to form hydroxonium ions, H3O+.

HCl(aq) -> H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)

H2SO4(aq) -> 2H+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq)

**Basicity** is the number of replaceable hydrogen ions one molecule of the acid produces.

- Monobasic: HCl, HNO3, CH3COOH
- Dibasic: H2SO4, H2CO3, H2S
- Tribasic: H3PO4

Note that ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, has four hydrogen atoms but only the one in the carboxyl group is replaceable, so it is monobasic.

blocks.title: Strong is not the same as concentrated
blocks.text: Strength describes how completely an acid ionises: a strong acid such as HCl ionises almost fully, while a weak acid such as ethanoic acid ionises only slightly. Concentration describes how much acid is dissolved in a given volume. You can have a dilute solution of a strong acid and a concentrated solution of a weak acid.

blocks.markdown:
## Bases and alkalis

A **base** is a substance that neutralises an acid to give a salt and water only. Metal oxides and metal hydroxides are the common examples.

An **alkali** is a base that is **soluble in water**. All alkalis are bases, but only the soluble ones are alkalis. NaOH, KOH and aqueous ammonia are alkalis; CuO and Fe(OH)3 are bases that are not alkalis.

An **amphoteric oxide or hydroxide** reacts with both acids and alkalis. Aluminium, zinc and lead compounds behave this way:

- ZnO + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2O (acting as a base)
- ZnO + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2O (acting as an acid)

blocks.title: Identifying conjugate acid-base pairs
blocks.prompt: In the reaction HCl + NH3 -> NH4+ + Cl-, identify the Bronsted-Lowry acid, the base and the two conjugate pairs.

steps.text: Find what happens to the proton. HCl loses an H+ and becomes Cl-, so HCl is the proton donor and therefore the acid.
NH3 accepts that H+ and becomes NH4+, so ammonia is the proton acceptor and therefore the base.
A conjugate base is what remains after an acid has donated its proton. The conjugate base of HCl is Cl-.
A conjugate acid is what forms after a base has accepted a proton. The conjugate acid of NH3 is NH4+.
Each pair differs by exactly one H+, which is the quick way to check your answer.

blocks.answer: HCl is the acid and NH3 the base; the conjugate pairs are HCl/Cl- and NH3/NH4+

items: Acids turn blue litmus red; alkalis turn red litmus blue
Acids have a sour taste; alkalis taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery
Acid solutions conduct electricity because they contain mobile ions
Neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali is always exothermic
Concentrated acids are corrosive and must be added to water, never water to acid

blocks.title: Salt plus water only
blocks.text: The phrase 'salt and water only' is what separates a base from a carbonate. Carbonates also neutralise acids, but they release carbon dioxide as well, so they are not classified as bases. Examiners test this distinction almost every year.

points: An Arrhenius acid gives H+ in solution; a Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton.
Basicity is the number of replaceable hydrogen ions per molecule of acid.
Strength refers to the degree of ionisation, concentration to the amount dissolved.
A base neutralises an acid to give salt and water only; an alkali is a soluble base.
Amphoteric substances such as ZnO and Al2O3 react with both acids and alkalis.
Acids react with metals to give hydrogen and with carbonates to give carbon dioxide.
